In brief

Parody. "Pride of Calpe's rocky mount [...] Marion of the bountiful bosoms": the Cyclops narrator's leering response to the news that Blazes Boylan is organizing the concert tour prompts an opposite, troubadour-like tribute to Molly's Mediterranean charms. The bountiful bosoms remind one of the narrator's crass carnality, but the preceding sentences inhabit an atmosphere of rarified exotic beauty.

At more length

Molly is the "Pride of Calpe's rocky mount, the ravenhaired daughter of Tweedy." Calpe is a name for Gibraltar that is no longer used, though a Mediterranean Spanish town some distance to the northeast bears the name today. (It too is located next to a big rock.) Mons Calpe, "Mount Calpe," was the ancient Roman (originally Greek) name for the Rock of Gibraltar that looms over the British settlement where Brian Tweedy raised his daughter. The air of poetic wonderment begun by identifying Molly as the "Pride of Calpe's rocky mount" continues by calling her "ravenhaired"—jet black, glossy, deep as night. Her beauty is "peerless"—this word hearkens back to the earlier parody in which aristocratic elegance radiated from "a godlike messenger," "an elder of noble gait and countenance," and "a dame of peerless lineage, fairest of her race." Exotic "loquat and almond scent the air"—loquat trees came to the Mediterranean from China and Japan, and almond trees from Iran, much as Molly's opoponax perfume hails from Somalia and Arabia. In "The gardens of Alameda" (a Spanish word applied to tree-lined promenades and the parks associated with them) "the garths of olives knew and bowed" to Molly, recognizing and honoring a great lady. (A garth, according to the OED, is simply "a small piece of enclosed ground.")

All of this high-toned adoration contrasts jarringly with the narrator's crude certainty that Boylan is "the bucko that'll organise her," and the parody concludes with an ironic glance at the unromantic reality: "The chaste spouse of Leopold is she: Marion of the bountiful bosoms." Bloom's wife is hardly chaste, and to the men in the bar her large breasts deserve something more than reverential bowing.

Gifford believes that this passage and the single sentence about J. J. O'Molloy and Ned Lambert that follows it make up a single unit, one that "Parodies nineteenth-century reworkings of medieval romance." Terence Killeen regards them as separate parodies, as do I. The two paragraphs look in different directions—one back to the discussion of Molly's concert tour, the other forward to the two men now entering the bar. And although both passages romantically exalt their subjects, the character of the writing is quite different. O'Molloy and Lambert are starkly cast as heroes in the mold of "O'Bloom, the son of Rory." Molly is described much more sensuously as a creature of exotic sundrenched lands.

John Hunt 2026
